title: Herbs and Spices for Arthritis: Evidence and Safety

content:
Quick answer: Enjoy herbs and spices for flavour, but do not treat them as proven arthritis medicines. Studies of concentrated supplements do not establish that adding a spice to a meal relieves joint pain. Evidence for turmeric and ginger supplements is uncertain, and herbal products can cause side effects or interact with medicines. Check the exact product with a pharmacist before taking it, and keep following your prescribed arthritis care.

Cooking ingredients and supplements answer different questions

A pinch of cinnamon in porridge, a ginger capsule and a concentrated turmeric shot are different exposures. The plant name alone does not tell you the dose, ingredients or formulation. A study of an extract cannot tell us how much of a food spice to eat for a similar effect.

Laboratory findings also need care. A substance changing an inflammatory pathway in cells or animals does not establish that it reduces pain, improves daily activities or prevents joint damage in people with arthritis. A change in a blood marker is not the same as a benefit you can feel.

For osteoarthritis, NICE identifies therapeutic exercise, weight management if appropriate, and information and support as core care. Herbs and supplements should not displace that care. If you have inflammatory arthritis, do not stop or reduce prescribed disease-controlling treatment to try a product. Ask your rheumatology team about symptoms that remain difficult.

Turmeric and curcumin: a cautious reading of the evidence

A Cochrane review published on 19 November 2026 included nine studies with 1,245 people, all with knee osteoarthritis. The studies lasted four weeks to three months; the evidence search was current to 7 November 2025.

Compared with placebo, turmeric supplements may produce little to no improvement in pain, function or quality of life. The average extra pain improvement was 0.72 points on a 0-to-10 scale. There was a small improvement in participants reporting treatment success. Confidence in these results was low, and the effects on adverse events were very uncertain.

Older summaries, including the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), describe initially positive findings but also call for better-quality evidence. Different products and study methods help explain why headlines vary. Neither summary establishes a reliable benefit for every product, rheumatoid arthritis, or turmeric used in cooking.

More absorption is not automatically better

Some curcumin products contain piperine from black pepper or other ingredients intended to increase absorption. That is not a reason to recommend an enhanced-absorption product. The UK Committee on Toxicity says formulation can alter potential toxicity and describes rare, unpredictable liver injury in supplement users. It distinguishes normal dietary use from higher exposures and supplements.

There is no need to add black pepper to turmeric for an arthritis treatment effect. Use spices to taste rather than chasing absorption percentages. Show any concentrated or enhanced-absorption product to your pharmacist, especially if you take regular medicines. Our turmeric and methotrexate guide explains why supplement safety and individual interaction advice are separate questions.

Ginger: possible benefit, limited confidence

NCCIH says ginger supplements might help knee osteoarthritis symptoms, but much of the research is poor quality. Most health studies have tested supplements rather than foods. This is not evidence that ginger tea works like ibuprofen, or that a particular kitchen quantity will relieve arthritis.

Ginger can be used for flavour if it suits you. Concentrated products can cause abdominal discomfort, heartburn, diarrhoea or mouth and throat irritation. If you take medicines, ask a pharmacist before using a ginger supplement. A product being natural does not settle whether it is suitable for you.

Cinnamon, garlic, rosemary and green tea

Cinnamon

NCCIH finds no clear support for using cinnamon for a health condition. Ordinary food amounts differ from larger or prolonged supplement use. Some cassia products contain substantial coumarin, which can be a concern for susceptible people, including those with liver disease. Choosing Ceylon cinnamon is not a way to turn it into a proven arthritis treatment.

Garlic and rosemary

Use them as ingredients you enjoy, rather than as a treatment prescription. This guide does not recommend a daily number of cloves, a rosemary-oil joint remedy or a supplement regimen. Claims about laboratory mechanisms or associations between diet and arthritis cannot establish that taking a garlic or rosemary product treats your joint symptoms.

Do not assume an extract, essential oil and a food ingredient are interchangeable. For supplements and herbal remedies, the NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service (SPS) advises checking the actual ingredients, formulation, medicines list and individual circumstances. Garlic and ginger products are among those it flags for possible bleeding concerns around surgery. Tell your surgical team what you take and ask when to stop or restart it; do not alter prescribed medicines yourself.

Green tea

A drink and an extract are different products. NCCIH notes that green tea contains caffeine, while extract supplements can have side effects and medicine interactions. Rare liver injury reports mainly concern extracts in tablets or capsules. This page does not recommend green tea, matcha or an extract as an arthritis treatment or set a daily therapeutic cup target.

Make food enjoyable without buying a treatment promise

If you like these flavours, try ginger in a stir-fry, garlic or rosemary in a soup, or cinnamon on porridge or baked fruit. These are meal ideas, not tested arthritis doses. You do not need to buy a supplement or a special blend to use herbs in cooking.

Choose a small change that fits your taste, budget and ability to prepare food. Ready-chopped, frozen or dried ingredients can be practical alternatives. If gripping or chopping is difficult, see our daily living guide for ways to approach kitchen tasks. Keep any dietary restrictions or individual advice from your healthcare team.

A pharmacist checklist before taking a product

  • Bring the label or a clear photograph. Include the brand, all ingredients, amount per dose, suggested daily amount, and any piperine or enhanced-absorption claim.
  • List everything else you use. Include prescriptions, bought painkillers, vitamins, teas, powders and other supplements. Tell the pharmacist when you started each product.
  • Explain your circumstances. Mention pregnancy or breastfeeding, liver or kidney problems, and planned surgery. The NHS advises against herbal medicines in several of these situations; do not treat an online guide as clearance to take one.
  • Ask what benefit is realistic. Is there evidence for your condition and this formulation? What would count as worthwhile improvement, and what is the cost?
  • Agree what to watch for. Ask about side effects, interactions, follow-up and when to stop the product. There is no universal four-to-twelve-week trial that is safe or useful for every supplement.

SPS notes that interaction evidence is often limited to theory or case reports. Missing information is not proof of safety. A traditional herbal registration (THR) mark relates to quality and traditional use; it does not prove an arthritis benefit. Do not stop prescribed medicine without talking to the prescriber.

When not to wait for a food change

NHS septic arthritis guidance advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for sudden severe joint pain, swelling, skin colour change or difficulty moving a joint, especially if you feel unwell or shivery. Fever is not always present. Do not wait to see whether a spice helps.

Stop a turmeric or curcumin supplement and seek medical advice promptly if you develop possible liver-injury symptoms such as yellow eyes or skin, dark urine, nausea, poor appetite or unusual tiredness. Tell the service the exact product and your medicines. NCCIH describes these warning symptoms. Follow the healthcare professional's advice about prescribed treatment rather than changing it yourself.

Can herbs replace arthritis medicines?

No. Do not stop or reduce prescribed arthritis treatment to use a herb, spice or supplement. If treatment is not meeting your needs or is causing side effects, ask your pharmacist, GP or rheumatology team for a review.

Does better absorption prove a supplement works better?

No. A formulation that increases exposure has not automatically shown a worthwhile clinical benefit or lower risk. Product ingredients, evidence and safety need separate checks.

Do I need to avoid spices in ordinary meals?

A warning about concentrated supplements is not a blanket instruction to avoid normal food seasoning. Follow your own dietary advice, avoid ingredients that cause a reaction, and check if you are unsure whether a drink, powder or extract counts as a concentrated product.

Sources checked for this editorial revision on 19 November 2026. Fresh qualified clinical review remains pending. This guide is general information, not a supplement prescription or a personal interaction check.
